title: Effect of an Intervention — Placeholder Seed

concepts.objective: Explain what it means to intervene on a variable, as distinct from merely observing it at a value.
Describe the average treatment effect as a population-level contrast between two intervention values, distinct from any single individual's outcome.
Identify a confounder as a common cause of treatment and outcome, and explain how adjusting for it can recover an intervention effect from observational data.
Explain why an intervention effect is identifiable from observational data only together with causal assumptions, and not from data alone.

sources.citation: Peters, Jonas; Janzing, Dominik; Schölkopf, Bernhard. Elements of Causal Inference: Foundations and Learning Algorithms. MIT Press, 2017.

claims.proposition: An intervention on a variable is modeled by replacing that variable's own structural assignment (its causal mechanism) with a new rule, such as fixing it to a constant, while every other variable's mechanism stays as it was.

source_refs.locator: Section 3.2 (Interventions), paragraph introducing hard interventions and the do(·) notation

claims.proposition: Setting a variable to a value by intervention can produce a different distribution over the rest of the system than simply observing that variable at the same value.

source_refs.locator: Section 3.2, Example 3.2, equation (3.4) (conditioning differs from intervening)

claims.proposition: An average treatment effect is defined as the difference between the average outcome the population would have if everyone were assigned one intervention value and the average outcome if everyone were assigned another.

source_refs.locator: Section 3.2, Example 3.2 (comparing the intervention distributions of E under do(C:=2) and do(C:=3))

claims.proposition: A population-level intervention contrast is not the same quantity as the change in outcome for any single individual, since individuals can respond differently even when the population-level contrast is fixed.

source_refs.locator: Section 3.2, Example 3.2 (intervention distributions describe the population under do(·), not one unit)

claims.proposition: A confounder is a variable that causally influences both the treatment and the outcome, and this shared cause can make treatment and outcome statistically associated even when adjusting for the confounder would remove or change that association.

source_refs.locator: Section 3.2, equation (3.4) (the observational conditional distribution differs from the intervention distribution)

claims.proposition: When the variables that confound a treatment and an outcome are known and measured, conditioning on them (adjusting for them) can make the resulting observational contrast match the intervention effect, closing the gap between conditioning and intervening.

source_refs.locator: Section 3.2 (Interventions), general discussion of do(·) versus conditioning on observed values

claims.proposition: An intervention effect is identifiable from observational data only in combination with a set of causal assumptions, because the same observational distribution can be compatible with more than one causal model that disagree about the effect of intervening.

source_refs.locator: Section 4.1.1 (Why Additional Assumptions Are Required), Proposition 4.1

claims.proposition: No amount of purely observational data can pin down an intervention effect on its own if the causal assumptions needed to identify it, such as no unmeasured confounding, are not also supplied.

resources.text: A researcher wants to know what would happen to plant growth if watering were doubled. She personally sets each plant's watering amount to a fixed schedule, overriding whatever the usual gardening routine would have produced. What has she done, in causal terms?
Ask whether the new watering rule was already going to happen naturally, or whether it replaced how watering was normally decided.

Intervening means replacing a variable's own causal mechanism with an external rule, leaving the rest of the system's mechanisms unchanged. This is different from picking out cases where the variable happened to take that value on its own, which is why an intervention and an observation at the same value can lead to different outcomes.

Yes. Fixing the watering schedule herself replaces the normal mechanism that decides watering, while the plant's growth response to water stays the same, which is exactly what defines an intervention.

Treating this as ordinary observation misses the key difference: an intervention overrides the mechanism that would have produced the value, so it can behave differently from a case where that value simply occurred on its own.

A university wants to know how much a new teaching method would change average exam scores if every student used it, compared to if every student used the old method instead. Which quantity are they trying to estimate?
Ask whether the quantity of interest is about one specific student's outcome or an average outcome across the whole population under each intervention.

The average treatment effect contrasts the average outcome under one intervention value with the average outcome under another, across the whole population. It is a population-level quantity, not a statement about how any particular individual would respond.
Yes. Comparing the average score under 'everyone gets the new method' with the average score under 'everyone gets the old method' is precisely the average treatment effect.
One student's change in score after switching methods is an individual outcome, not the population-level contrast that the average treatment effect describes.

A clinic finds that patients who take a vitamin supplement have lower rates of illness. It turns out that health-conscious patients are both more likely to take the supplement and more likely to exercise and eat well, which independently reduces illness risk. What role does 'health consciousness' play here, and what could help isolate the supplement's own effect?
Ask whether a variable can be a common cause of both the treatment and the outcome even though it occurs earlier in time than the treatment.

Health consciousness causally affects both taking the supplement and getting ill, so it is a confounder: it can make the supplement and illness look associated even apart from any effect of the supplement itself. If health consciousness is measured, comparing patients within similar levels of it (adjusting for it) can bring the observational contrast closer to the true intervention effect of the supplement.

Yes. Health consciousness is a common cause of both taking the supplement and getting ill, and adjusting for it is the standard way to try to recover the supplement's own effect from observational data.

A variable does not need to occur after the treatment to confound it; a common cause that occurs earlier, like a stable disposition such as health consciousness, can still bias the observed association between treatment and outcome.

Two analysts look at the exact same observational dataset relating a drug to recovery. One assumes there is no unmeasured confounding and concludes the drug increases recovery; the other allows for a plausible unmeasured confounder and finds the data are equally consistent with the drug having no effect at all. What does this disagreement illustrate?
Ask whether a single joint distribution over the observed variables can be produced by more than one underlying causal model that disagree about the effect of intervening.

The same observational data can be compatible with different causal models that make different assumptions, such as whether an unmeasured confounder exists, and those models can disagree about the intervention effect. The effect only becomes identifiable once specific causal assumptions are added; without them, no amount of observational data settles the question.
Yes. The two analysts made different causal assumptions, and because the observational data alone cannot rule either assumption out, the same data are consistent with different intervention effects.

Neither analyst has necessarily made an arithmetic error. A single observational dataset can be compatible with more than one causal model, and those models can imply different intervention effects, so the disagreement can come entirely from differing assumptions rather than a mistake.

choices.text: She has intervened on the watering variable: she replaced its normal causal mechanism with an external rule, while the plant's other causal relationships, such as how growth responds to water, stay the same.
She has simply observed a natural case where watering happened to be high, so this is really the same as picking out the high-watering days from the record.
The average treatment effect: the difference between the average score the population would have under 'everyone gets the new method' and under 'everyone gets the old method.'
The improvement that the single best-performing student experienced after switching methods.

Health consciousness is a confounder: it causally affects both taking the supplement and getting ill, and adjusting for it, such as by comparing patients with similar health consciousness, can help recover the supplement's own effect.
Health consciousness is irrelevant here, because it existed before the supplement was taken and something that comes earlier cannot confound a later treatment.

The intervention effect is not identifiable from the observational data alone; it depends on which causal assumptions, such as the absence of unmeasured confounding, are added, and different assumptions can fit the same data while implying different effects.
One analyst must have made an arithmetic mistake, since the same dataset can only support one correct effect estimate.
